Scope reading as recon step zero
recon

Description

This bug focuses on scope reading as recon step zero so you can verify whether This day is about discovery that produces clear, prioritized testing hypotheses instead of endless raw lists. The first useful artifact is often the program policy, not the first subdomain..

Reproduce / Process

  1. Read the program scope and list only the domains, hosts, and asset types that are allowed.
  2. Collect public leads from passive sources like search results, certificates, archives, or public subdomain data.
  3. Open the live hosts in the browser and note login pages, APIs, uploads, dashboards, or other interesting features.
  4. Group the findings into high, medium, and low-priority testing targets.
  5. If a forgotten or sensitive public asset is still accessible, save the URL and why it matters.

Impact

Discovery mistakes can hide forgotten assets or enlarge the testing queue with unvalidated leads.

Mitigation

Keep scope records explicit, retire forgotten assets, and maintain a repeatable workflow that turns discovery into validated priorities.

Evidence / Variants:
  • Convert every clue into a testing hypothesis
  • Keep scope notes beside asset lists
Sources: ProjectDiscovery Subfinder · ProjectDiscovery httpx

Email-security recon: SPF, DMARC, MX context
email-security

Description

This bug focuses on email-security recon: spf, dmarc, mx context so you can verify whether This day is about mail-related trust signals and how organizations communicate security expectations through their messaging setup. Mail records help explain what trust the organization expects around messaging..

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the domain you are reviewing and open a trusted email-security checker or DNS lookup page.
  2. Check the domain for SPF, DMARC, MX, and related mail records.
  3. Compare the result with what users are expected to trust from password-reset or notification emails.
  4. Note whether the records are missing, weak, or misconfigured.
  5. If the mail trust setup is weak, save the lookup result and the account workflow it can affect.

Impact

Weak mail trust can support spoofing, confuse users during recovery flows, and reduce confidence in account-security notifications.

Mitigation

Harden SPF and DMARC alignment, send trustworthy account notifications, and align email-based trust with actual application security controls.

Evidence / Variants:
  • Focus: Email-security recon: SPF, DMARC, MX context
  • Preserve the smallest reproducible proof with clear scope.
Sources: OWASP Authentication · ProjectDiscovery dnsx

Description

This bug focuses on prioritizing auth-heavy surfaces so you can verify whether This day is about discovery that produces clear, prioritized testing hypotheses instead of endless raw lists. Settings, billing, support, onboarding, and recovery features are often richer than marketing pages..

Reproduce / Process

  1. Read the program scope and list only the domains, hosts, and asset types that are allowed.
  2. Collect public leads from passive sources like search results, certificates, archives, or public subdomain data.
  3. Open the live hosts in the browser and note login pages, APIs, uploads, dashboards, or other interesting features.
  4. Group the findings into high, medium, and low-priority testing targets.
  5. If a forgotten or sensitive public asset is still accessible, save the URL and why it matters.

Impact

Discovery mistakes can hide forgotten assets or enlarge the testing queue with unvalidated leads.

Mitigation

Keep scope records explicit, retire forgotten assets, and maintain a repeatable workflow that turns discovery into validated priorities.

Evidence / Variants:
  • Convert every clue into a testing hypothesis
  • Keep scope notes beside asset lists
Sources: ProjectDiscovery Subfinder · ProjectDiscovery httpx
DAY 088 API discovery and endpoint grouping Recon & Surface Mapping 1 bug block ▶
Phase: Recon & Surface MappingResearch expansion dayHands-on reproduce block included
Days 17-160 ke liye reproduce/process blocks ko aur simple, repo-style, step-by-step format me rewrite kiya gaya hai taaki practice flow easy lage.
API discovery and endpoint grouping
api

Description

This bug focuses on api discovery and endpoint grouping so you can verify whether This day is about API-specific trust and whether direct endpoints behave more loosely than the visible UI suggests. Group APIs by auth model, object type, rate-limit posture, and business criticality..

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the URL https://target.com and login using the desired credentials.
  2. Open the feature that calls the API and capture the request in DevTools or Burp.
  3. Send the request to Repeater and change only one value like role, object ID, method, or hidden field.
  4. Forward the modified request and compare the API response with what the UI allows.
  5. If the API performs more than the UI should permit, save the endpoint, modified request, and response.

Impact

API-only trust gaps can expose actions and data paths that the visible UI appears to protect.

Mitigation

Align API authorization with business rules, validate object ownership server-side, and keep endpoint exposure consistent with UI permissions.

Evidence / Variants:
  • Compare UI-limited fields with direct endpoint behavior
  • Artifacts: endpoint path, object ID, auth context
Sources: PortSwigger API Testing · OWASP API Security

Evidence capture standards
reporting

Description

This bug focuses on evidence capture standards so you can verify whether This day is about turning validated behavior into a professional, reproducible, and appropriately-scoped report. Capture enough detail that another reviewer can reproduce the behavior cleanly..

Reproduce / Process

  1. Pick one completed day from this series and open the notes, screenshot, and request evidence you saved.
  2. Write the title, affected feature, reproduce steps, impact, and mitigation in separate blocks.
  3. Reduce the reproduce steps until they become one clean path anyone can follow.
  4. Add only the evidence needed to prove the issue and remove extra noise.
  5. If the report is still understandable after cutting the noise, keep that version as your final template.

Impact

Weak documentation increases the chance of triage confusion, duplicates, or under-scoped fixes even when the underlying bug is real.

Mitigation

Standardize titles, steps, impact, remediation, and retest notes so every validated issue is easy to reproduce and fix.

Evidence / Variants:
  • Keep title, scope, proof, impact, fix, retest clearly separated
  • Prefer one minimal reproduction over noisy bulk evidence
Sources: Bugcrowd VRT · OWASP WSTG

Daily practice routine design
habit

Description

This bug focuses on daily practice routine design so you can verify whether This day is about building a sustainable system that makes learning and reporting sharper over time. Small repeatable loops beat random tool-heavy bursts..

Reproduce / Process

  1. Pick one day from your recent practice and reopen the notes you wrote for it.
  2. Check whether the note includes the URL, account state, reproduce steps, impact, and mitigation.
  3. Rewrite the note in a shorter and cleaner format if any important piece is missing.
  4. Move repeated lessons into a reusable checklist for the next practice session.
  5. If the cleaned note is easier to repeat after a few days, keep that format as your daily standard.

Impact

Poor note and review discipline makes future bugs harder to reproduce, explain, prioritize, and learn from.

Mitigation

Keep notes normalized, tag recurring weak areas, and review a small amount of evidence every day instead of storing unstructured bulk.

Evidence / Variants:
  • Store one reusable note or checklist every day
  • Review misses, not only wins
Sources: PortSwigger Web Security Academy · Bugcrowd VRT

GraphQL introspection exposure
graphql

Description

This extension day focuses on graphql introspection exposure so you can verify whether inspect whether introspection, schema metadata, or hidden object names reveal more than the role should learn.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the URL https://target.com and login using a low-privileged test account.
  2. Open the feature that sends GraphQL requests and capture the /graphql request in DevTools or Burp.
  3. Repeat the same request and change only the field list, object ID, nested object, or batch shape.
  4. Send the modified request and compare the response with what the low-privileged user should be able to access.
  5. If extra data, actions, or hidden schema details are returned, save the query, response, and affected role boundary.

Impact

Resolver or schema mistakes can leak hidden fields, bypass object controls, or multiply attack surface through a single endpoint.

Mitigation

Restrict schema exposure where appropriate, enforce authz per resolver, and cap batching, depth, and complexity for risky operations.

Evidence / Variants:
  • Watch introspection, nested fields, batching, mutation scope
  • Artifacts: query shape and unauthorized field
Sources: OWASP GraphQL · PortSwigger GraphQL

JWT algorithm and key-trust review
token

Description

This extension day focuses on jwt algorithm and key-trust review so you can verify whether confirm tokens are verified with the expected algorithm, key, and trust path.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the forgot-password, invite, magic-link, or verification flow of the target.
  2. Trigger the link using your own test account and receive the token in your mailbox.
  3. Use the link once and note the normal success behavior.
  4. Now reuse the same link again, or generate a newer link and retry the older one.
  5. If the reused or older token still works, save the token flow, final response, and the account impact.

Impact

Reusable or overlong-lived tokens can extend trust beyond its intended moment and may lead to unauthorized account or workflow control.

Mitigation

Scope tokens tightly, expire them quickly, rotate them on re-issue, bind them to the intended action, and reject reuse server-side.

Evidence / Variants:
  • Variants: reset, invite, verification, magic link
  • Evidence: issued-at time, reuse attempt, server response
Sources: OWASP JWT · OWASP Session Management

OAuth redirect URI validation
auth

Description

This extension day focuses on oauth redirect uri validation so you can verify whether make sure delegated login returns only to explicitly trusted redirect destinations.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the login or connect-account flow that uses OAuth or SSO.
  2. Start the flow normally once and capture the redirect URL, state value, and callback request.
  3. Repeat the same flow and change only the redirect destination, state handling, or linked account condition in your authorized test setup.
  4. Complete the callback and compare whether the server accepts the changed state safely.
  5. If the wrong account is linked or the callback trusts an unsafe value, save the start URL, callback request, and final account result.

Impact

Broken identity gates can grant access, verification state, or recovery power before the server has enough proof to trust the user.

Mitigation

Enforce account-state checks on the server, require verification before privileged features, and keep identity transitions explicit and auditable.

Evidence / Variants:
  • Compare: guest vs unverified vs verified vs recovered
  • Evidence: session issuance, state change, protected route access
Sources: OWASP Authentication · OWASP OAuth2

Email-change confirmation race
race

Description

This extension day focuses on email-change confirmation race so you can verify whether test whether concurrent or out-of-order confirmation flows let the wrong email remain trusted.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the one-time action like coupon apply, email change confirm, reset complete, or another limited workflow.
  2. Complete it once normally to know the expected final state.
  3. Repeat the same action from two tabs or two captured requests at nearly the same time in your authorized test setup.
  4. Refresh the account or object state after both requests complete.
  5. If the application accepts both requests when only one should succeed, save both requests and the inconsistent final state.

Impact

Broken concurrency control can let repeated requests bypass one-time rules, limits, balances, or approval sequences.

Mitigation

Enforce atomic state transitions server-side, use idempotency controls, and serialize sensitive updates that should only happen once.

Evidence / Variants:
  • Artifacts: request count, timing, final inconsistent state
  • Choose one-time actions and counters
Sources: PortSwigger Race Conditions · OWASP WSTG

Description

  2. Complete the process once normally so you know the valid order of steps.

Role-change permission persistence
access-control

Description

This extension day focuses on role-change permission persistence so you can verify whether check whether stale permissions survive when the user role or team membership changes.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Create two test accounts and login to them in two separate browsers.
  2. Using Account A, open the target feature and capture the request that updates or reads the object.
  3. Copy the object ID or account-linked value from Account A.
  4. Using Account B, replay the same request while replacing its object value with Account A data.
  5. If Account B can read or modify Account A data, save both account states, the changed object ID, and the response.

Impact

Broken access control threatens confidentiality, integrity, and privilege boundaries across users, roles, and objects.

Mitigation

Enforce object ownership and role checks on every backend action instead of assuming the UI constrained the request.

Evidence / Variants:
  • Use two accounts or two roles
  • Focus on ownership-changing actions and admin-only surfaces
Sources: OWASP API Security · PortSwigger Access Control

Second-factor weaknesses undermine the extra trust layer that should protect account takeover and sensitive state changes.

Mitigation

Keep factor proof server-side, protect recovery and reset flows with strong re-verification, and prevent client-side state from deciding success.

Evidence / Variants:
  • Look at enroll, reset, recovery, trusted-device flows
  • Evidence: missing proof step or client-side success control
Sources: OWASP WSTG

Description

This extension day focuses on secret scanning and history review so you can verify whether inspect code, artifacts, and history for keys, tokens, or unsafe config patterns.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the public page, JavaScript file, debug route, mobile bundle, or client config related to the feature.
  2. Open DevTools Network tab and inspect the loaded assets one by one.
  3. Search the response bodies for hidden routes, keys, debug flags, source maps, or environment details.
  4. Compare whether the exposed data should really be visible to a normal user.

  • Look for hidden APIs, roles, or environment names

Duplicate triage and variant grouping
reporting

Description

This extension day focuses on duplicate triage and variant grouping so you can verify whether practice separating true duplicates from meaningful variants that deserve separate fixes.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Pick one completed day from this series and open the notes, screenshot, and request evidence you saved.
  2. Write the title, affected feature, reproduce steps, impact, and mitigation in separate blocks.
  3. Reduce the reproduce steps until they become one clean path anyone can follow.
  4. Add only the evidence needed to prove the issue and remove extra noise.
  5. If the report is still understandable after cutting the noise, keep that version as your final template.

Impact

Weak documentation increases the chance of triage confusion, duplicates, or under-scoped fixes even when the underlying bug is real.

Mitigation

Standardize titles, steps, impact, remediation, and retest notes so every validated issue is easy to reproduce and fix.

Evidence / Variants:
  • Keep title, scope, proof, impact, fix, retest clearly separated
  • Prefer one minimal reproduction over noisy bulk evidence
Sources: Bugcrowd VRT · OWASP WSTG

  2. Check whether the note includes the URL, account state, reproduce steps, impact, and mitigation.

Poor note and review discipline makes future bugs harder to reproduce, explain, prioritize, and learn from.

Mitigation

Keep notes normalized, tag recurring weak areas, and review a small amount of evidence every day instead of storing unstructured bulk.

Prompt injection review for AI assistants
ai-promptOWASP GenAI inspired

Description

This day focuses on whether user input, pasted content, uploaded files, or retrieved context can steer an AI assistant away from its intended safety or access rules.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the AI assistant, chatbot, search helper, or summarizer feature using your own authorized test account.
  2. Ask one normal question first so you can see the expected safe response style.
  3. Now submit user content, pasted instructions, or retrieved context that tries to change the assistant behaviour in your authorized test setup.
  4. Compare whether the system follows the application rules or starts obeying the injected instructions instead.
  5. If the assistant ignores its intended boundaries, save the prompt flow, attached context, and final response.

Impact

Prompt injection can make an AI feature ignore safety rules, expose hidden context, or misuse connected tools beyond the intended workflow.

Mitigation

Separate untrusted content from trusted instructions, add strong policy checks before tool use, and review high-risk prompts with defense-in-depth controls.

Evidence / Notes:
  • Check prompts, uploaded docs, pasted text, browser content, and retrieved knowledge separately.
  • Preserve the normal-safe response and the injected response side by side.
Sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 2026 · OWASP Prompt Injection
DAY 162 Improper AI output handling AI & LLM Security Awareness 1 bug block ▶

AI aur LLM security ke ye extra days simple, step-by-step, authorized review ke liye add kiye gaye hain.
Improper AI output handling
ai-outputOWASP GenAI inspired

Description

This day reviews whether AI-generated output is trusted too much by downstream renderers, automation, or other application components.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the feature where AI output is shown, exported, rendered, or passed into another system.
  2. Generate one normal result first and note how the application handles it.
  3. Repeat with a response that contains unusual formatting, links, markup, or structured fields in your authorized test setup.
  4. Check whether another viewer, renderer, or workflow trusts the AI output without validation.
  5. If downstream handling gives the AI output too much trust, save the prompt, output, and affected follow-up action.

Impact

Unsafe handling of model output can turn one untrusted response into downstream rendering, workflow, or automation risk.

Mitigation

Treat AI output as untrusted input, validate it for the destination context, and require explicit server-side checks before actions or rendering.

Evidence / Notes:
  • Good targets: HTML preview, markdown preview, email generation, JSON actions, exports, and auto-filled forms.
  • Capture both the raw model output and the later place where it is consumed.
Sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 2026 · OWASP Improper Output Handling
DAY 163 Sensitive data leakage in AI responses AI & LLM Security Awareness 1 bug block ▶

Sensitive data leakage in AI responses
ai-disclosureOWASP GenAI inspired

Description

This day checks whether the AI feature reveals secrets, private records, system prompts, or internal context that the current user should never receive.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the AI feature using a normal low-privileged test account.
  2. Ask a normal business question first and record the expected safe answer.
  3. Now ask follow-up questions about internal notes, hidden instructions, other users, or previous conversation data in your authorized test setup.
  4. Compare whether the response stays inside the current user permission boundary.
  5. If protected data appears in the answer, save the prompt chain, response, and the exact data class that leaked.

Impact

AI response leakage can expose private user data, internal system details, business secrets, or hidden instructions to the wrong person.

Mitigation

Minimize sensitive context in prompts, filter outputs before display, apply strict data-access controls, and log high-risk leakage patterns for review.

Evidence / Notes:
  • Check chat history isolation, hidden prompt content, RAG snippets, and cross-user memory.
  • Redact any real secret before storing evidence.
Sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 2026 · OWASP Sensitive Information Disclosure
DAY 164 Agent tool authorization drift AI & LLM Security Awareness 1 bug block ▶

Agent tool authorization drift
ai-agentOWASP GenAI inspired

Description

This day reviews whether AI agents or tool-calling assistants can trigger actions that exceed the current user role, scope, or approval path.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the agent or assistant feature that can call tools, actions, or connected services.
  2. Use a normal low-risk request first and note which action the system is expected to perform.
  3. Repeat with a request that could touch another user, a sensitive action, or a wider scope in your authorized setup.
  4. Check whether the tool call still respects the current role, object ownership, and approval boundary.
  5. If the agent performs more than the user should be allowed to do, save the prompt, tool action, and resulting state change.

Impact

Weak authorization around agent tool use can let a model trigger actions that the user never had direct permission to perform.

Mitigation

Apply the same server-side authorization checks to every agent action, require approvals for sensitive operations, and keep least-privilege tool scopes.

Evidence / Notes:
  • Compare chat permissions with direct API permissions.
  • Record both the user role and the tool action actually executed.
Sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 2026 · OWASP Excessive Agency
DAY 165 Excessive AI agency and auto-action risk AI & LLM Security Awareness 1 bug block ▶

Excessive AI agency and auto-action risk
ai-agencyOWASP GenAI inspired

Description

This day focuses on AI features that can send emails, edit records, file tickets, or trigger business actions without strong confirmation and scope limits.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the AI workflow that can take actions such as sending, updating, creating, or approving something.
  2. Run the feature once with a small safe action so you understand the normal approval path.
  3. Now request a broader action in your authorized test setup and watch whether the assistant asks for confirmation, scoping, or justification.
  4. Compare the requested action with the final action that actually happens.
  5. If the system performs an over-broad action without proper confirmation or limits, save the request, approval path, and final effect.

Impact

Over-broad AI agency can create unauthorized changes, accidental data exposure, or unintended business actions at machine speed.

Mitigation

Use explicit approvals, least-privilege scopes, action previews, and server-side policy checks before any real-world change is committed.

Evidence / Notes:
  • Look closely at email senders, ticket creation, record updates, and payment-like actions.
  • Keep evidence of what was asked versus what the agent really did.
Sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 2026 · OWASP Excessive Agency

RAG and vector store access control
ai-ragOWASP GenAI inspired

Description

This day checks whether retrieval-augmented generation brings back documents, embeddings, or knowledge chunks that the current user should not be allowed to see.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the AI search, assistant, or document-chat feature that uses uploaded knowledge or internal content.
  2. Ask about a document you are supposed to access and note the normal retrieval result.
  3. Now ask about another team, another user, hidden documents, or broader collections in your authorized test setup.
  4. Compare whether the retrieved snippets stay inside the current permission boundary.
  5. If cross-tenant or over-broad knowledge is returned, save the query, snippet source, and affected document scope.

Impact

Weak retrieval controls can expose private documents, internal notes, or cross-tenant knowledge through otherwise helpful AI answers.

Mitigation

Bind retrieval to user and tenant permissions before context is assembled, re-check source access server-side, and limit broad collection queries.

Evidence / Notes:
  • Compare direct document permissions with AI retrieval permissions.
  • Capture the quoted snippet and its original document scope.
Sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 2026 · OWASP Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
DAY 167 Model denial of service and unbounded consumption AI & LLM Security Awareness 1 bug block ▶

Model denial of service and unbounded consumption
ai-dosOWASP GenAI inspired

Description

This day looks at whether AI features allow runaway token usage, excessive retries, huge context windows, or cost-heavy operations without sensible guardrails.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the AI feature that accepts free-form text, long documents, or repeated generation requests.
  2. Use one small request first and note the normal speed, size, and visible limits.
  3. Now try larger but still safe test inputs, repeated requests, or repeated regeneration in your authorized setup.
  4. Watch whether the application enforces quotas, request size limits, cooldowns, or cost controls.
  5. If the AI path allows unusually high consumption without checks, save the request size, repeat count, and system response.

Impact

Unbounded AI consumption can cause slowdowns, outages, high cost, and reduced availability for legitimate users.

Mitigation

Set server-side quotas, input limits, timeout controls, concurrency limits, and account-level usage monitoring for expensive AI operations.

Evidence / Notes:
  • Measure latency, visible limits, retries, and billing-like guardrails.
  • Prefer controlled safe tests over massive load.
Sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 2026 · OWASP Unbounded Consumption

Data and model poisoning awareness
ai-poisoningOWASP GenAI inspired

Description

This day reviews whether fine-tuning data, uploaded knowledge, or trusted corpora can be polluted in ways that degrade the model or bias later answers unsafely.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the workflow where documents, examples, feedback, or knowledge sources are added to the AI system.
  2. Add one normal safe item first so you understand the expected ingestion flow.
  3. Now review whether low-trust contributors, weak moderation, or hidden instructions inside data could influence later answers in your authorized setup.
  4. Check whether the system validates and reviews what becomes trusted AI context or training material.
  5. If low-trust data can silently shape later output or retrieval, save the ingestion path, trust boundary, and resulting behaviour change.

Impact

Poisoned AI data can distort later answers, weaken safety controls, or cause harmful business decisions at scale.

Mitigation

Review training and retrieval inputs, isolate trust levels, require moderation or approval for sensitive data sources, and monitor drift in model behaviour.

Evidence / Notes:
  • Focus on ingestion trust, contributor roles, moderation, and later answer changes.
  • Keep a baseline answer and a changed answer for comparison.
Sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 2026 · OWASP Data and Model Poisoning
DAY 169 System prompt leakage review AI & LLM Security Awareness 1 bug block ▶
Phase: AI & LLM Security AwarenessAI / LLM review daySimple reproduce/process block

System prompt leakage review
ai-prompt-leakOWASP GenAI inspired

Description

This day checks whether hidden system instructions, internal rules, or protected assistant context can be exposed to normal users through conversation or connected content.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the AI assistant using a normal user account and ask one regular question first.
  2. Now ask about hidden rules, system instructions, internal policies, or previous hidden messages in your authorized test setup.
  3. Repeat after giving the assistant uploaded text, pasted content, or retrieved context that tries to expose hidden instructions.
  4. Compare whether the response reveals internal prompt content or secret control text.
  5. If hidden instructions or protected context appear, save the prompt chain, answer, and the exact class of leaked internal content.

Impact

System prompt leakage can reveal internal logic, hidden controls, safety assumptions, or secret operational details that help later abuse.

Mitigation

Minimize sensitive prompt content, isolate secrets from prompts, filter outputs, and design the system so hidden instructions are not directly recoverable by users.

Evidence / Notes:
  • Test direct questions, uploaded context, and follow-up prompt chaining separately.
  • Redact any sensitive leaked text before storing it.
Sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 2026 · OWASP System Prompt Leakage
DAY 170 AI overreliance and unsafe automation sign-off AI & LLM Security Awareness 1 bug block ▶
Phase: AI & LLM Security AwarenessAI / LLM review daySimple reproduce/process block

AI overreliance and unsafe automation sign-off
ai-governanceOWASP GenAI inspired

Description

This day focuses on whether the product lets users or staff trust AI output too much without human review for security-sensitive, financial, or identity-impacting actions.

Reproduce / Process

  1. Go to the AI-assisted workflow that helps with support, approvals, fraud review, coding, moderation, or another important decision.
  2. Complete one normal task first and observe what human review is expected before the result is trusted.
  3. Now look for places where the AI answer can be accepted, sent, or executed too quickly in your authorized setup.
  4. Compare the risk of the decision with the amount of human review actually required.
  5. If security-sensitive output can be trusted too easily, save the workflow, review gap, and the downstream decision that could be affected.

Impact

Overreliance on AI can turn inaccurate or unsafe outputs into real user harm, bad approvals, leaked data, or insecure operational decisions.

Mitigation

Require human review for high-risk outputs, show confidence or provenance where appropriate, and keep AI suggestions separate from automatic execution.

Evidence / Notes:
  • Look for one-click accept, auto-send, auto-approve, or silent trust in AI summaries.
  • Document the human review step that should exist but does not.
Sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 2026 · OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
